idiom_name: object Empty : Type (object declaration) / data object inside a sealed interface
implementation_notes: An object declaration implements the interface and is the single instance of the special case, so the classic subclass-plus-singleton pair collapses into two lines; inside a sealed hierarchy the same idea is a `data object Empty : Account`, which adds sane equals/toString for the degenerate case, and a `when` over the sealed type makes handling exhaustive. The standard library does exactly this for collections - emptyList() returns the single internal EmptyList object. Kotlin's null safety removes many cases outright (a non-null property cannot be 'unset'), so use the special case for genuine domain states and a nullable type with `?:` when the caller must decide.
pitfalls: Object declarations are initialised lazily on first access: a special case whose init block registers, logs or touches other objects will do that at the first use, not at startup.
Extension functions are dispatched statically, so a 'default no-op' added as an extension on the interface is not overridable by real implementations and may win or lose depending on the static type.
A `when` over a sealed hierarchy without an else branch breaks compilation when a variant is added - intended, but a source-compatibility cost for published libraries.
Passing a Kotlin object to Java code exposes it as a singleton instance; interfaces with default methods may then be shadowed differently than expected across the boundary.
